topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Reduce repeated stored data when many objects contain the same stable details. The attached EPUB uses many rendered objects and shared tree types. Before adding a pool, identify substantial duplicate state and measure whether sharing helps. Flyweight is a memory design with lookup and lifetime costs, not a rule that every repeated value needs another class.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Separate shared identity from per-use state.
Use immutable shared objects with a complete lookup key.
Explain memory tradeoffs and shared lifetime.

blocks.text: Separate intrinsic state, which many uses can share, from extrinsic state, which describes one use. A pool finds the shared object by a complete key. Contexts retain a connection to that object while keeping their own changing details. The shared object must remain stable for all contexts; a change made for one context must not silently change every other context.

cards.question: What problem does Flyweight address?
cards.answer: Reduce repeated stored data when many objects contain the same stable details. The attached EPUB uses many rendered objects and shared tree types. cards.question: What is Flyweight?
cards.answer: A design that shares repeated state while keeping per-use state separate.

cards.question: What is Intrinsic state?
cards.answer: State that belongs to the shared object identity and can be reused across contexts.

cards.question: What is Extrinsic state?
cards.answer: State that belongs to one use of a shared object.

cards.question: What is Interning?
cards.answer: Reusing one stored object for repeated requests with an equal identity key.

cards.question: What is Immutable?
cards.answer: Not changing after construction.

cards.question: Why would storing position x inside the pooled Style break this design?
cards.answer: Two marks needing the same appearance but different positions would either overwrite each other or require separate styles, defeating the chosen shared-state boundary.

cards.question: Why is const Flyweight& f = factory.GetFlyweight(...) not proof of sharing in the attachment?
cards.answer: GetFlyweight returns by value. The reference binds to a temporary produced by a deep copy, not the pooled entry. Our shared_ptr copies handles while preserving the shared object.

topics.title: Repeated data can outweigh useful differences
topics.summary: A drawing tool places many marks on a page. A mark has a style name, a style size, and a horizontal position. Thousands of marks may use the same style while each position differs. For a few marks, store all three fields directly in every object. That is simple, clear, and often the right answer.

blocks.text: The limitation appears when the shared portion becomes large. Imagine that a style later contains a loaded shape outline or a rendering table. Copying that payload for every mark may consume far more memory than the positions themselves. Before changing the design, measure the repeated data and the number of uses. Our small program keeps style data intentionally short so the ownership mechanism is visible; it is not evidence that this tiny representation saves memory.

topics.title: Split stable shared data from each use
topics.summary: Flyweight is a memory-sharing design that stores repeated state once and gives each use a connection to it. The shared state is called intrinsic state. Here name and size identify the style. The state that belongs to a particular use is called extrinsic state. Here x is the mark's position. A Mark holds a shared style owner and its own x value. Two Marks can therefore agree on style without becoming the same mark.

blocks.text: StylePool looks up a style by a Key containing both name and size. If that key already exists, it returns another shared owner of the same Style object. Otherwise it creates one immutable Style, stores an owner in the map, and returns another owner. Reusing an existing object is often called interning. It is useful only when equality of the chosen key truly means the shared data is interchangeable.

The key is a std::pair<std::string, int>, not two fields joined into an unstructured string. A pair keeps field boundaries unambiguous. If a later style includes color, color must become part of the key too. A pool keyed only by name would wrongly reuse dot size twelve for a request for dot size twenty. The visible mistake would be a correct position with the wrong style size.

topics.title: Read the shared pointer type carefully
topics.summary: StylePtr is an alias for std::shared_ptr<const Style>. shared_ptr means several owners can keep the same object alive. const Style means the object reached through this owner is read-only. It is not the same as const shared_ptr<Style>, which would prevent reseating that particular pointer variable but would still permit changing the Style through it.

blocks.text: The pool constructs the object with make_shared<const Style>. The actual allocated Style is const, not merely viewed through one const handle while another mutable handle is retained. Its fields are initialized once and then read. Immutability means the object does not change after construction. That matters because a mutation to one shared style could otherwise change every mark using it. The public fields remain safe to read because access is through a pointer to const; the pool gives out no mutable owner.

A shared_ptr copy increments a shared ownership count; it does not copy the Style. When one pointer is destroyed, the count decreases. The object remains alive while at least one owner remains. The pool owns styles through its map, and each Mark owns its style through style_. This is shared ownership, so an ownership diagram must not imply that a mark exclusively owns its style. The arrows are labeled shared owner to make that distinction explicit.

topics.title: Trace a lookup and a draw
topics.summary: main requests (dot,12) twice. The first lookup misses, creates one Style, and stores it. The second lookup finds the existing entry and returns found->second, which is the map's shared_ptr value. first and same therefore point to the same object. A request for (dot,20) uses a different key and receives a different object. The pointer equality checks test identity, not merely equal field values.

blocks.text: Mark left takes an owner of the twelve-size style and stores x = 3. Mark right receives another owner of that same style and stores x = 8. draw reads the shared name and size, then appends its own position. The outputs dot/12@3 and dot/12@8 show the separation directly. Neither draw call changes the style or the other mark.

In draw, const auto& name borrows the string inside Style while the Mark's owner keeps the Style alive. const auto size copies the small integer. Both are suitable choices: copying an int is cheap; copying the string is unnecessary for this local read. The returned formatted string is a new owned value. It does not expose a reference into shared state and remains valid after the Mark is destroyed. Mark explicitly defaults its copy operations, which suppresses automatic generation of move operations. Constructing from std::move(left) therefore copies the shared owner; both marks stay usable. This value-like policy avoids a moved-from Mark with a null style.

topics.title: Lifetime is independent of the pool scope
topics.summary: The program creates a short-lived StylePool inside a nested scope and saves one returned owner in survivor outside that scope. When the pool is destroyed, its map releases its owner. survivor still owns the Style, so reading survivor->name afterward is valid. This test checks a real advantage of shared ownership: the pool's lifetime need not enclose every use.

blocks.text: The pool uses strong owners, so it also retains each style until the pool is destroyed or entries are removed. An unused style does not vanish merely because its last Mark disappears. That is a cache-retention policy, not a leak caused by missing delete. A long-running application may require a size limit, explicit clearing, or weak_ptr entries. A weak pointer observes a shared object without keeping it alive, but it requires checking whether the object still exists before reuse. That complexity should be justified by actual retention needs.

The compiler checks const access and pointer types; it cannot prove that the key includes every meaningful field. At runtime, map lookup compares keys and finds a matching entry. std::map lookup takes logarithmic comparisons in the number of styles. shared_ptr adds a control block and ownership bookkeeping. Neither cost disappears because the design has a name.

topics.title: Calculate the tradeoff before calling it an optimization
topics.summary: Suppose N marks each have U bytes of unique state and would otherwise carry S bytes of shared payload. The direct representation costs roughly N times (U + S), ignoring container and allocation overhead. With K distinct styles and a per-mark handle of H bytes, sharing costs roughly N times (U + H) plus K times S, plus pool and control-block overhead. When K is nearly N or S is tiny, sharing may lose. When S is large and K is much smaller than N, it can win substantially.

blocks.text: This example does not report exact saved bytes because object layout, string storage, allocator overhead, and platform details matter. Measure the real workload. Also test semantic isolation: changing a mark's position must not change another mark, and equal style keys should share exactly when that is part of the pool contract. Flyweight is a targeted optimization, not a reason to turn every small value into a shared pointer.

topics.title: Worked example: contracts and alternatives
topics.summary: Several marks, one immutable style

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Share styles only when both name and size match.
Keep each mark position separate.
Reject empty names, size outside 1–100, and missing style pointers.

blocks.text: A map interns immutable Style objects by a complete structured key. shared_ptr allows marks to retain styles after a pool is destroyed.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: One active pool returns the same object for the same key.
Published Style objects are immutable.
Each Mark owns its own position and shares only intrinsic style state.

blocks.text: Alternative: Store style fields by value for a small number of small styles. Integer style IDs into a stable central table can use less per-mark memory but require a clear table lifetime and ID-validity contract.

Verification: Tests verify same-key identity, different-key separation, distinct positions, size boundaries, invalid size, null-style rejection, survival beyond a pool lifetime, and safe copying even from an rvalue expression. The program does not benchmark memory savings or synchronize concurrent pool access.
Maintenance: Share measured heavy immutable data. Keep the key, lifetime policy, and per-use state obvious so later fields do not accidentally change sharing semantics.

blocks.title: Solution reasoning
blocks.text: The solution clears the map. Existing shared_ptr owners keep old styles alive. The next request creates a new equal-valued object because the old entry is absent. This is a deliberate pool-lifetime identity rule: sharing is guaranteed among active entries, not across every clearing operation for the entire process.

workshop.pitfall: Use only name as the pool key. A request for dot/20 can incorrectly receive the existing dot/12 style. The key does not include all intrinsic state.

discussion.question: There are twenty marks and every style is a short integer code. Compare by-value storage with shared_ptr flyweights.
discussion.answer: By-value integer codes are likely simpler and smaller. Flyweight is worth considering when the repeated payload is large and reused often. Measure memory and workload before introducing allocation, lookup, and shared ownership.
discussion.hint: The handle and control block have costs too.

workshop.alternative: Store style fields by value for a small number of small styles. Integer style IDs into a stable central table can use less per-mark memory but require a clear table lifetime and ID-validity contract.
workshop.design: A map interns immutable Style objects by a complete structured key. shared_ptr allows marks to retain styles after a pool is destroyed.
invariants: One active pool returns the same object for the same key.
Each Mark owns its own position and shares only intrinsic style state.
workshop.maintenance: Share measured heavy immutable data. Keep the key, lifetime policy, and per-use state obvious so later fields do not accidentally change sharing semantics.

overview.title: Shared style, separate positions
overview.explanation: Each hollow-diamond link is explicitly labeled shared owner, rather than exclusive composition. Both marks reach the same immutable Style but keep separate x members. The pool keeps another strong owner. A reference count tracks these owners; the Style is destroyed only after the last strong owner releases it. The diagram uses shared aggregation to show the non-exclusive relationship; the C++ shared_ptr contract supplies the precise lifetime rule.
